LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Train — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson builds a train out of kitchen chairs: chugging, tickets, one engine and a station — with tracks-not-roads as the quiet fact riding along.

What is this?

A train is a long vehicle that runs on tracks and goes choo choo — a chain of carriages your toddler can count, hook and drive.

What does it mean?

One train, many carriages: the train is where part-and-whole shows up in a toddler’s favourite machine. Counting carriages is counting with a purpose.

What does the child need to know?

Trains go on tracks, cars go on roads — one sentence, said while pointing at wheels and rails, files itself away. Real platforms have the loud announcements and the gap.

Why this matters

No other card arrives with its own soundtrack quite like this one. Few games convert a rainy afternoon into forty minutes of organised noise as reliably as the chair-train.

What it teaches

Sequencing and pretend roles (driver, passengers, inspector), sound chains in rhythm, and the tracks-versus-roads distinction that organises the whole vehicle world.

Words to learn

trainchoo chootrackcarriagestationticket

Say this to your child

“"A train! Choo choo! Can you chug with me? Chugga-chugga-choo-choo! Here comes our train, running on tracks, not roads. All aboard! Tickets, please — next stop, the kitchen!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say train, then choo choo — with slow arm-wheels and a chuffing breath.
  2. Build the chair-train: kitchen chairs in a line, your toddler as the engine at the front, chugging around the room together.
  3. Hunt trains in books and toy boxes; count the carriages on each one — one, two, three.
  4. When the sound comes out as a chuff or a woo, take it and add one more choo; chains grow one link at a time.
  5. Ride the real thing this week if you can — the platform gap, the whoosh, the doors — or run the chair-train daily and sell tickets.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows the label Train with Choo choo written below. Ask how many carriages are hooked behind the engine, then count them together.

Ask your child

"Where is the train?" "What does the train say?" "Does the train go on tracks or on the road?" "Who is driving our train today?"

What your child can say or do

"Choo choo!" plus a chugging march, or a ticket held up high for clipping. Expect the chair-train to run daily for weeks — engines do not retire quickly.

Out in the real world

Station platforms are train heaven: the announcement, the whoosh, the gap between train and edge. Behind the yellow line, hand in hand, the real thing beats every card.

Try it together

Full service: driver, passenger and ticket inspector, with paper tickets punched by a grown-up. The station is the sofa; the destination rotates; the announcements are yours to invent.

Understanding check

Ask what the train says and where trains go — tracks or roads. A choo choo plus tracks passes. The chair-train appearing unprompted is the distinction between passed and owned.

Parent tips

Let your toddler be the engine first — leading the chug gives them the tempo, and tempo is what makes the sound chain survive. Keep tickets scrap-paper simple; the punching is the joy.

Staying safe

Real platforms are the danger zone: hand held, behind the line, before the train is even visible. At home, the chair-train needs its cushions checked for trip-hazards before departure.

This lesson pairs with the Train flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).
